about: What this plugin is known not to hold. A limit written only in prose is lost the next time someone reads past it, so every one of them has a row here and the row is checked. `where` names the records that state it: `dNNNN` a decision record, `spec` the specification, `handoff` the handoff page, `escapes` the escapes ledger, `trials` the trial protocol. `plan` is the disposition the owner locked on 2026-11-13; a row never silently changes plan. Closed rows stay, so that a claim can be checked against what closed it.

areas.guide: The skill that walks a person through the layers of a new design system.
areas.adopt: The skill that records what a repository already has, without changing it.
areas.audit: The read-only report on how far a repository has got.
areas.find: The read-only search of the store, nearest store first, before something new is built.
areas.inventory: The read-only inventory of the store: what each store holds, the state of each piece, six kinds of finding, and what it could not look at.
areas.intake: The command that takes a block into the store for a need, by the ladder of three rungs, every choice the owner's on the decision sheet.
areas.status: The read-only report on what waits on the owner and what to run next.
areas.decide: The sheet of every question that waits on the owner, and the answers written back.
areas.document: The document a command hands over, set on the frame every document shares.
areas.checks: The gate tool and the browser test it installs.
areas.rules: The page a screen-building agent reads before it starts.
areas.specimen: The sheet that draws the options on the repository's own screen.
areas.book: The handoff book drawn from the repository.
areas.reference-app: The example application this repository carries as its proof.
areas.trials: The runs by independent agents that test the plugin.
areas.upgrade: The command that brings the installed tool into a repository, the stamp it writes, and the version it compares.

kinds.partial-check: A check holds less than the ledger row it proves claims.
kinds.no-check: A rule is written down and nothing holds it.
kinds.wrong-signal: A report or a check can mislead the person reading it.
kinds.stack-bound: It works only on one kind of repository.
kinds.unproven: It is built, but nothing independent has exercised it.
kinds.conflict: Another document in the system tells a builder the opposite.

plans.fix: Meant to be closed by this project; the roadmap says when.
plans.keep: Accepted as it is, stated here so nobody counts on more.
plans.hand-off: The fix belongs to another repository, named in `repo`.

limits.note: The contrast check covers two pairs of the primary colour only, while the audit counts the row as fully held by the machine.
Nothing measures the contrast of a hover or pointer state; the one real failure was caught by accident.
Target size is read as a height from source classes only, so a control narrower than the threshold still passes.
For column width and table density the machine holds only that no screen overrides them, yet the audit counts both rows as held.
Nothing forces a screen with an action done at once to declare a failure state, so a screen that swallows the error passes.
The focus check only asks that something holds focus, so focus landing on the wrong thing passes.
An adopted brand colour is not pinned, so swapping it for another colour that also meets contrast passes.

The token file carries colour, corner radius and type only: there is nothing for font, spacing, elevation or motion.
The component reader matches the floor's way of writing components rather than parsing them, so a component written another way is listed without its variants.

limits.note: A control that declares no height of its own is not measured at all, and appears in the register as a control with no height.
Turning a class into pixels assumes the framework's four-pixel unit, so a repository that declares another unit gets wrong numbers.
A column's width is counted in digit widths, so a text column is only approximately right, and the starting sample lengths are a machine proposal.
No rule says how each column type is formatted, edited in place or filtered, and a number printed without the formatter is caught by nothing.
The states row holds that a screen declares its states, not that it draws them.
The check for words written into a screen misses text built by joining strings, and alignment set on an element nested inside a cell still slips through.
An error message is recognised only through the floor's alert component, so a repository that reports errors any other way gets no row.
The states row depends on the floor's list of screens, so a repository without that file gets no states row.
The notification row holds only that no screen goes around the repository's own module; which message belongs on which channel is a person's review.
Four rules for what follows an action live on the rules page with no check: the list changing in place, undo, the empty state, and moving between screens.
Import direction holds only where a screen-kind page exists, does not follow an import through a package, and lets two files inside one part import each other.
Three rules have no check: at most two buttons on a row, each row waiting on its own, and the ledger being only for shared rules.
The narrow-width check measures the sample data only: a name longer than about twenty-two characters would turn it red, and no state carries one.
Only the head of a screen-kind page is read; the order of information and the prose in its body are checked by nobody.
A screen that builds its own overlay or a separate record page is caught by nothing, and a record opened while the list still loads does not take focus.
The table of evidence a repository may already have recognises the floor's lint rules only, so a repository with its own must write those rows by hand.
Adopt installs the value checks only where the repository's gate collects the included make files; another shape of gate gets self-declared rows.
The threshold that decides a repository has a brand colour of its own is a machine guess, so a tinted grey can be overwritten.
A ledger row records no confidence in its check, and has no pointer kind for a data type, another linter, or the acceptance kit's own grading.
Which layer each standard decision belongs to is a machine judgement nobody has challenged; four edge cases carry a note instead.
The audit cannot tell a decision nobody has made from one made somewhere its ledger does not record.
The sheet can only show what the reference implementation happens to use, and the swatches and size list that make up for it are drawings from values, not real components.
Pictures are not the same to the pixel across machines; only the list of options, their values and the page itself are.
Whether the book looks good can only be judged by a person, and three of its eight sheets have never been looked at.
The book's list of what it shows leaves out the pictures and the words on screens, so a stale picture still reads as matching.
Fonts are not carried in the book, four components that need a parent are not drawn at all, and two others are drawn bare.
What the page for the list kind of screen says is a machine proposal the owner has not confirmed.
Whatever was fixed after the most recent trial has not been tried by an independent agent, which is true by construction after every trial.
An independent agent cannot look at a sheet on a person's behalf, so the parts chosen by eye have no agent-run acceptance.
The test that builds an empty repository borrows this repository's real stylesheet and Makefile, and the full gate only ever runs here.
There is a continuous-integration file but no remote, so every check has only ever run on one machine.
limits.closed_by: the repository has a remote and its first continuous-integration run passed the whole gate; the tests that need the two neighbouring repositories are skipped there

limits.note: The token measurement this project promised has never been run, and the earlier claim that the plugin saves tokens was withdrawn as unfounded.
The independent critique's largest risk, that this is a reskin of a component library that already supplies values and components, has never been answered.
The plugin does not touch rework caused by tests or infrastructure, and cannot say whether the experience it produces is any good.
The wording of the guide's questions is policed by a list of words to avoid, not by requiring every term to be in the vocabulary.
This repository has declared nothing to the acceptance kit, so the kit's own tier has not moved although both artifacts exist.
The repository's guide for agents does not mention the plugin folder, because that file belongs to the tool that laid the repository.
The language and the currency of the example application were inferred by machine and nobody has confirmed them.
Nothing fails when a trial is run and no row is added to the series, so the numbers depend on the session remembering.
The standard brief runs against a repository that keeps growing, so two runs of it are not strictly the same task.
The floor's three browser tests carry no decision tag, so no ledger row can point at them and the accessibility check runs twice here.

Floor documents tell a builder the opposite of approved rules on column width, on locking a button, on a link dressed as a button, on installing a component, and on the widths the browser checks run at.
Colours written in the perceptual notation slip past the acceptance kit's comparison of raw colours against tokens, which reads hexadecimal only.

Status counts what waits in the ledgers and in the waiting list, so a question that waits somewhere else, such as a pull request, a conversation or a page of prose, is not counted and the report can say nothing waits while something does.
Status counts the questions of the waiting list and not the permissions it lists, which only the owner gives step by step, so the count can be nought while the owner still has something to allow.
A finding of a document carries its evidence in words only, while the specification asks for a picture wherever one can be drawn, so a reader cannot see the place a finding speaks of.

The design audit report has no chapter on accessibility conformance and cannot be printed for that chapter alone, which the specification asks for, because no list says which standard decisions are about accessibility.
A document becomes a pdf only through a browser found in the packages of the target repository, so a repository without one gets the page alone and the call ends with work left.
Two pdf files printed from the same page differ in their bytes, because the browser writes the moment of printing into the file, so only the page is the same byte for byte.
A document prints the labels of the frame and the words of its command in English only, and the words file a repository keeps for the handoff book does not reach it.
A document is dated by the last commit of the repository and not by the day it was made, so one made from work not yet committed carries an earlier date and only a mark beside its revision says so.
No recommendation of a document rests on a design principle yet, because no command records the principles an owner fixed, so every reason given is a measurement or a standard.
The status report writes out the first five questions that wait and names the rest, as the screen does, so the recommendation for the others is only on the decision sheet and in the data.
Whether a document looks good and reads well only a person can judge, and the owner has looked at neither the status report nor the design audit report.

The specification gives upgrade a --remove that takes the plugin out of a repository, and this version leaves it out: removing the tool, its gate step, the ledgers it writes and the rows that point at it is more than a small addition, so a repository that wants the plugin gone removes it by hand.

Upgrade writes the tool folder, the stamp and the ledgers the tool writes, and not the gate step mk/design-assembly.mk beside them, so a change the plugin makes to its gate step reaches no repository that adopted it before; upgrade says when that file differs, and writes nothing to it.

The gate upgrade calls green or red is the design-assembly step of the repository's gate, run in its process on the repository as the upgrade would leave it, so a test of the repository's own that imports the tool, or any other step of its make check, can turn red after an upgrade that said green.

Which decisions change state is read by running the repository's own copy of the tool for the state before and the installed tool for the state after, so a copy too old to say how each row is held, or one that cannot be run, gives no before, and upgrade then says it cannot tell instead of listing them.

On a checkout whose dependencies are not installed, a stylesheet that imports a library's palette cannot be resolved, so the preview says the tokens ledger would lose its entries and the gate would turn red. It stops and writes nothing, which is right, but it names the ledger and a contrast check as the cause instead of the missing dependencies; on a fresh branch of the reference repository it listed 37 tokens as lost until npm ci ran.

The gate that makes the plugin's version go up compares the trees of its templates and its scripts, so a change to a skill, a reference list or the README reaches a person under the same version number, and an installed plugin is not told a newer one has other words.

On a repository with no Makefile that includes the make files of mk/ and collects their CHECK_TARGETS, adopting writes nothing at all, and its message names only the include line, so a repository not born from repo-setup cannot reach the gate or an upgrade without reading the templates.

Installing the plugin from a folder on the machine copies that folder's working tree, untracked files included, while the record of the install names a commit, so what is installed is not exactly that commit.

The installed copy's README points to tests, make targets and an example application that exist only in this repository, and one shipped test reads three folders above itself, so a person who reads them from the installed plugin finds nothing there.
The page of checks names make targets for status and decide that the gate step adopting installs in a repository does not have, so those commands run only through the plugin's own path there.

For the product type and the conformance level, status and decide recommend only that a person answer, though the guide has its own default for the conformance level, so the sheet asks without saying what the machine would choose.
Only the component manifest can be kept out of git. The design tokens file and the column types file are derived too and stay in git; nothing offers the choice for them.

A manifest kept out of git is written by the gate or by make design-components. Whatever reads it earlier on a clean checkout, such as a test that runs before the gate or another tool, finds no file, or an old one, and is not told why. Seen on a copy of a real repository whose gate runs its tests before the design step, 2026-11-16: five tests in three files failed on a clean clone, all green once the manifest was written.
limits.closed_by: derived.mjs writes every derived file a repository keeps out of git, and the plugin's make step runs it before make test when the tests are a step of the gate; what still misses it is limit derived-files-not-written-for-a-runner-alone

limits.note: Keeping the manifest out of git needs two steps in git that the command only names: the ignore line and taking the file out of the index. Until a person does both, the gate is red.

An acceptance kit that reads the design floor's tier from files on disk asks for the component manifest to be there. On a fresh worktree of a repository that keeps the manifest out of git, the file is not there until something writes it, so the kit reads the lower tier and names the manifest as missing. Seen on a copy of a real repository, 2026-11-16.

A derived file kept out of git is written by the gate, by derived.mjs and by the plugin's make step before make test. A test run by its runner alone, as an acceptance kit runs one test file, gets none of them, and on a clean checkout finds no file. The make step also reaches no repository through upgrade, which does not write it (limit upgrade-leaves-gate-step).

When the tool data names another path for the ledger of screens, the copy kept out of git follows the ledger to the new path, and the copy at the old path stays on disk, ignored by git and no longer written. A reader of the old path then reads an old ledger and is not told. The copy of the intake ledger is left the same way.

Once the ledger of screens is kept as one file per screen, a tool or a test of the repository's own that reads the one file finds none. The command gives the ledger as one text on demand, but nothing writes it to the old path before such a reader runs; a derived file kept out of git and written by the gate, as the component manifest is, is not built. Seen on a copy of a real repository, 2026-11-16: 99 tests in seven files and two other steps of its gate failed after the split. limits.closed_by: a repository may keep a copy of the ledger as one file at the old path (screen-fragments.mjs --copy), derived from the folder, out of git, written by the gate, by derived.mjs and before make test; what still misses it is limit derived-files-not-written-for-a-runner-alone

limits.note: The test the guide installed before this version imports the one file of the ledger of screens. After a split it fails on a missing file and does not say why, and the guide does not replace a test it installed once; a person deletes it and runs the guide again.

Kept as one file per screen, the screens are read in the order of their ids. The order a person gave them in the one file is not kept, and nothing lets a repository say another order. Seen on a copy of a real repository, 2026-11-16: a generated table the repository commits was written again in the new order, and two of its tests that expect the old order failed; nothing a user sees read the order. The intake ledger kept as one file per block is read the same way, in the order of its needs.

A ledger of screens is cut into fragments only when every id is plain letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore, and no two ids differ only by capitals. A repository whose ids carry a slash or letters with marks must rename them first; the command stops and says which.

The command cuts a ledger of screens by moving its lines, so it reads only a list of screens written in block style. A list written on one line is refused, and text that runs over several lines under one key is not understood, as the reader itself does not understand it. A note written at the margin of the list goes with the screen after it, also when a person meant it for the one before, and every line ends the way this tool writes lines.

Splitting and joining change files and never touch git. Committing the folder with the removal of the one file is left to a person, and a pull request open at the time, which still edits the one file, meets that removal once. The second look the command takes before it removes the one file, reading the fragments back and comparing every entry, has stopped no ledger tried so far: only the comparison itself is tested, on entries taken away by hand.

The test the guide installs finds the fragments through the bundler's own way of importing every file of a folder as text. A repository whose tests run without that bundler, or with a version that spells it otherwise, has to read the folder its own way.

Upgrade does not offer to cut a ledger of screens into fragments; a person runs the tool's own command after upgrading. On the reference repository only a copy of its ledger and its model was split and joined: its own tools and tests that read the one file, and the acceptance kit, were not run against the folder. The same holds for the intake ledger, which no real repository has split yet: only made-up ledgers were cut, held and joined.

The guide and adopting find the intake ledger only at design/intake.yaml. A ledger kept elsewhere, under a name in the repository's own language for instance, is held only once a person names its path under ledgers.intake in the shapes check, and the guide's next run writes the usual path there again. Renaming the file to the usual path removes the limit.

A repository that spells the keys of the intake ledger its own way says so with a keys line in the ledger. A ledger written before that has no such line and is read as missing every key the contract names. Whether a repository's own reader of the ledger takes the extra key was not tried.

Which screens a change reaches is read from imports. What a screen reaches while it runs without importing it is followed only where an adapter names the code the server runs on its own, as route handlers: a request to an address written as text, a module imported by a computed name, a component chosen by its name at run time, code a job or worker runs. A file reached that way and also imported by a page is taken to reach that page alone.

An import is followed when it is relative, starts with @/, or starts with an alias the repository's TypeScript settings map to one folder, as x/* to ./src/*. An alias the build declares elsewhere, or one mapped to several folders, is taken as the first folder or not at all: an import of the repository's own that names no file then cannot be followed, and every change of code asks for the whole suite.
Where the folders are the screens, the pages are looked for under src/app only. A repository that keeps its app folder at the top finds no page, and every change of code asks for the whole suite.

The command only says which screens a change reaches and gives a pattern for their tests. Nothing runs fewer tests on it yet: choosing what continuous integration runs is the repository standards' own work, and the browser tests of this repository are theirs to change.

The wall reads the root colour line as written in the stylesheet the tool data names: the last --primary of a top-level :root block. A --primary declared in a file the stylesheet imports is not read, and a --primary that points at another variable (var(--brand)) is not followed, so changing that variable changes the brand colour and the wall stays open.

The wall opens on an answered question of the waiting list, and cannot tell whether the owner or an agent wrote that answer: the file is data, like the answers file of the decision sheet (limit decide-cannot-tell-who-wrote-the-answers). The rules page forbids an agent to answer, and nothing holds it. Asking the owner on the hosting service before a pull request that adds a kind of screen or a brand colour merges is the repository standards' own work.

The total comparison reads the judgments a branch adds or changes against the main branch. A judgment already on the main branch that no person marked is not compared, nor is anything on the branch where the repository meets the plugin (the base has no decision ledger), nor anything in a repository with no commit yet. Comparing every row would turn every repository that adopted before 0.7.0 red, though its rows were written on a person's word.

The total comparison covers the choices a machine reads: values, components, kinds of screen, states, words and column types. How the parts of one screen are laid out, when no rule of the ledger names it, is not a choice it can see: an agent that settles such a layout alone is not caught.

Source that goes around a decision is found for four scales only, as the audit finds it: a raw colour, a type size, a spacing and a radius between square brackets. A value going around any other decision is the repository's lint rule to catch.

Outside git the wall and the total comparison compare nothing: both pass, and the gate prints that it did not compare. With git and no branch it can name as the main one, both fail rather than pass unseen. A shallow checkout, as continuous integration makes one, has its history fetched from the remote named origin: main, else master, never the branch the remote's HEAD points at. So both need that remote, a way to reach it within two minutes a call, and a main branch named main or master or named with "main" on either check in design/theme.json; without them both fail and say what git said. Fetching writes the remote's ref and the checkout's depth, so a shallow clone on a person's machine is deepened by the gate, to its whole history when it is longer than every step.

Nothing makes an agent ask: it queues a question with decide --ask because the rules page says so. A call it makes in code alone, with no row of the ledger and none of the files the wall reads, leaves no trace the gate can compare.

The total comparison reads a person's answer to a judgment from the row's own note: an agent that writes 'confirmed by NAME on DATE' into a row it wrote itself passes, and nobody was asked. The ledger has no other place for who answered (limit decide-answer-kept-in-the-note), and the rules page forbids an agent to answer; nothing holds it.

Of what the audit reports as a decision with no row, the gate reads only a test that names decision:ID for an id with no row. A proof the audit recognises from the plugin's list of known proofs, and a value that looks like a person's answer, need lists that do not travel with the installed tool, so the gate does not read them; the audit still reports them.

In a workspace repository whose screens live under apps/NAME/ and whose stylesheet lives under packages/NAME/src/styles/, the audit and status read only the src/ folder at the top: they print no stylesheet and 0 source files, the audit's next line says there is nothing to read, and status ends with 0 and nothing to run, while the UI package alone, given as --target, has a stylesheet with a primary colour of its own and 35 places that go around four scales; find and inventory read the components and screens of the same folders, so in such a repository find finds none of them and inventory counts none of them unless the package is given as --target.

On a package that keeps its screens in an app folder at its top rather than under src/, the audit reads 0 source files and prints no stylesheet under src/, yet in the same report quotes the primary colour of a stylesheet the component settings name outside the folder given, and calls color-role, type-scale, spacing and radius undecided, as if it had seen that nothing answers them.

The specimen and the guide's writer look for the stylesheet at src/index.css only, not at the one design/theme.json or the component settings name, so on an adopted repository whose stylesheet is src/app/globals.css they end with 2 saying there is no screen to draw and no design floor to build on.

Custom properties declared under :root inside an @layer block of an imported stylesheet are not read, so a colour role written as var(--x), with --x declared there, is reported as pointing nowhere, and the contrast of the primary colour is said to be unreadable rather than measured.

The check for words written into a screen reads a type parameter in a .tsx file, such as <TData extends Omit<...>>, as a tag that holds text, so adopting reports the labels decision as failing today in files that put no words on a screen.

The component library's files are known by the folders components/ui and components/reui, not by the ui alias the component settings give, so a package that keeps the library in src/components counts the library's own files as its own: bypasses of the type, spacing and radius scales are listed in its button, calendar, tabs and scroll area, and its toaster is reported as a screen that calls the toast library itself.

On a repository whose stylesheet declares no --primary, adopting rightly refuses the source colour of step two, and the ladder command stopped there with an uncaught error and its stack, printing no row for steps two and three and not saying whether the reference changed; past that point, its equal rows were said to mean the repository had already taken every rung.
limits.closed_by: the ladder writes a refused step as a line of its report and goes on, and says when equal rows mean adopting took nothing in; held by the ladder's test on a repository with no gate and no --primary

limits.note: The total comparison takes every decision:ID written anywhere in a test of tests/ as a proof of that decision, the text of a sample or a string under test included. A test that writes decision:a or decision:other as data fails the gate with a decision the ledger has no row for, though nothing proves it. Seen on the reference repository.

A ledger kept as one file per entry has a one-file copy outside git for the repository's own readers. The copy is written by the gate and by the tool's own command. A fragment edited since then leaves the copy older than the folder, and a reader that prefers the copy reads the old values with nothing to say they are old. Seen on the reference repository, where one reader preferred the copy and another read the folder.

The browser test waits for a state's words to be on the page and never asks that they were absent before its steps, so a state listed with words the page always shows, as a row's waiting state may be since the row's actions button puts none on the page, passes before the state is reached.

The rules page says the row's actions button keeps each row's clock so a screen writes no timer of its own, while the button tells the screen nothing of when it starts to say it waits and the browser test needs words on the page for that state, so a screen that lists it writes a second one-second clock beside the button's.

The rules page lets an empty state carry one link inside its words to where items come from, while the gate fails any screen that links to another screen of the application, so the one link the rule allows cannot point to the screen where items come from.
Nothing reports a word of the repository's words file that no code uses any more; three sample words of the reference application are unused today and every check passes.

No tool of this plugin fetches a source or pins it again: a pin is read as the repository keeps it, so an old pin is only reported, never brought up to date. The snapshot of a source is compared with its pin only when the source names the folder it is kept in; a source pinned by a version, or one that names no snapshot, is read without that comparison, and the reader says so.

An intake ledger that already kept a key of its own named from, taken, changed, retired or merged_into on a block, or before or values beside the blocks, with a value of another shape, fails the gate once the tool of 0.8.0 is in, and the gate names that key. Upgrade says so before it writes and stops. Renaming the key of the repository's own removes it; no repository known to this project is in that case.

Find matches the words of a need against the words of each piece, never their meaning: a need written in the repository's own language does not match a catalog written in English, and a piece described in other words than the ones asked for is near or not found at all.

The inventory finds one thing taken twice only when two blocks name the same item of the same source, two files hold the same bytes, or two files of the repository export the same name: two different ways of answering one need, written in other words, are not found.

The inventory proposes a component for the store of its repository when screens of that repository import it from inside one screen; a piece two repositories of the family both make is not seen until a family store exists.

A block taken from an outside source is reported changed only when the ledger keeps the hash of its file taken when it came in: a block recorded before that key existed is named among what the inventory could not look at, never reported.

The inventory reports nothing unused in a repository where one import cannot be followed, or where no entry of the frame of the application is found, because a piece only that import or that frame reaches would be called unused: one such import hides every unused piece of the repository, and the blind spots name it.

The candidates of a need are given to the owner as words, with the page of each in its source, never as a picture: drawing an item of an outside source needs the network and a browser, and waits for the second build stack.

After an item of an outside source is kept, the block's file is the one the caller names with --file: intake never runs the install line, so it cannot tell that file is what the line put there; the hash under taken is of the file as named.
The candidates are what find matches by words: a need written in the repository's language finds no item of a catalog written in English, and is offered only by hand.
